results.title: Credit Spreads: Default Rates and Recovery Rates (Part 1/2)
results.content: # Credit Spreads: Default Rates and Recovery Rates (Part 1/2). In the debt markets, **credit spreads** are a vital signal, revealing the risk premium investors demand to hold a risky bond over a "safe" benchmark like a U.S. Treasury. When default rates rise, credit spreads tend to widen as investors grow nervous about getting paid back. *Credit Spread = (Probability of Default) × (1 - Recovery Rate)*. * **Recovery Rate (RR)**: The amount of money recovered by the creditor expressed as a fraction of a bond's principal value at the time of default. Going back to our previous example, if a bond has an estimated 40% recovery rate, and the credit spread is 2.5%, the market is pricing in a 4.2% chance of default. But, by tracking default rates and recovery trends, investors can better decode what credit spreads are whispering about the market. Credit Spreads: Default Rates and Recovery Rates (Part 2/2).

To assist in loan pricing, Trepp collects weekly spreads from nationwide CRE balance sheet lenders across loan-to-value (LTV) buckets and property types. Trepp-i is a weekly spread survey that offers insights into capital availability and underwriting trends across the major property types, with data starting in 2010. For the week ending September 12, 2025, low loan-to-value (LTV) spreads were largely unchanged, leading into the September FOMC meeting. * Retail spreads were unchanged for the week at 168 basis points over 10-year treasuries and 4.5 basis points above the record tight last observed in February of 2022. Trepp-i tracks CRE loan spreads collected from a wide array of lenders from the previous week for multiple LTV ratios.
